Introduction to the Collection
This collection is about a single numerical observation and what follows from it. The observation
is that bound systems across an enormous range of scales — subatomic particles, planetary
orbits, biological organisms, galaxies — each return a characteristic timescale of approximately
one second when their mass, radius, and coupling are combined in a specific geometric way. The
collection asks what that observation means, what it can explain, and what it cannot.
The claim is not that one second is a universal constant in the way that the speed of light is. The
second is a human unit, derived from Earth's rotation and base-sixty numeration. The universe is
not calibrated in seconds. What the observation points to is narrower and more interesting: a
dimensionless ratio that recurs across the hierarchy. When the relation is reformulated in natural
units — removing seconds, kilograms, and meters entirely — every scale from the electron to the
galaxy converges on the same dimensionless coordinate, to within a few percent, over more than
forty orders of magnitude in mass and radius. The one-second value is the human projection of
that ratio. The ratio itself is structural.
Whether that structure is a coincidence, a selection effect, or a feature of the universe is the
question the collection raises and does not fully answer. The papers are careful to distinguish
what is established from what is hypothesized, and the revisions recorded in the first paper's
appendix — following an independent analysis by Evgeny Volynets — make that distinction
explicit.
The collection is in four parts, and each part takes the observation in a different direction.
The first paper, The Earth–Moon Distance as a Resonance Condition, develops the planetary-
scale case. It introduces a celestial effective action that plays the role of Planck's constant at the
Earth–Moon–Sun scale, shows that the present configuration satisfies the resonance condition to
within about two percent, and reports a second numerical fact: the actual Earth–Moon distance is
within 1.8% of the value that would make the resonance exact. The paper then asks whether that
near-match is a coincidence, a selection effect, or a structural feature of the dynamics.
The original draft of this paper claimed that the system sits on a dynamically stable plateau. That
claim was incorrect. Volynets showed that in the reduced isolated Earth–Moon model the
resonance function has a kinematic minimum, not an attractor, and that the present system is past
that minimum rather than at it. The revised appendix withdraws the plateau claim and separates
three things: what is observed, what is compared numerically, and what remains an open
dynamical question. The correction is recorded because it matters, and because the collection's
credibility depends on being clear about what it can and cannot defend.
The second paper, The Human Scale as a Resonant Node, places the human scale in the
hierarchy. The human effective action turns out to be the geometric mean of the quantum and
solar effective actions, and the human energy scale that follows is on the order of the mechanical
of 4 99
work of a heartbeat. The geometric means of particle and astrophysical masses bracket the
human mass range. The human scale is not imposed on the hierarchy; it emerges from it as the
natural intermediate node.
The third paper, The 1 Hz Resonance, takes the argument into biology. Denis Noble has argued
that the heartbeat's rhythm cannot be explained by genetic instruction alone — there is no master
clock in the genome. The paper proposes that the master clock is physical rather than genetic: the
heart beats at approximately one hertz because the particles that constitute cardiac tissue satisfy
the one-second invariant. The rhythm is not programmed; it is the natural inertial frequency of
the matter the heart is made of.
The fourth paper, The Large-Moon Condition, is the most recent and represents the culmination
of the collection. It shifts the focus from the numerical coincidence of the one-second value to a
physical anomaly: the Moon is exceptionally massive for a terrestrial planet. Its mass ratio to
Earth is an order of magnitude larger than that of any other satellite–planet pair in the Solar
System apart from the Pluto–Charon binary.
The paper argues that this mass ratio is the critical parameter, for two independent reasons. First,
a satellite of lunar mass stabilizes a planet's obliquity against chaotic variation — but only within
a window. A satellite somewhat more massive than the Moon would have destabilized Earth's
obliquity rather than stabilizing it. The large-moon condition is a window, not a threshold.
Second, the mathematical reduction of the celestial resonance shows that the condition scales
exactly with the cube of the mass ratio. The resonance is satisfied only for satellite-to-planet
mass ratios in a narrow range, and Earth is the only system in the Solar System that falls inside
it.
These two lines of evidence — the dynamical stability of the obliquity and the mathematical
satisfaction of the resonance — converge on the same physical parameter. That convergence is
the basis for the filter hypothesis advanced in the fourth paper: that the resonance condition may
act as a selection effect on planetary architecture, favouring worlds whose mass ratios are
simultaneously compatible with a stable climate and with the resonance condition. The filter
hypothesis is a middle position. It is more specific than the weak claim, because it makes a
prediction about which systems should host complex life rather than merely recording a
coincidence on Earth. And it replaces the strong claim of the earlier abiogenesis paper, which is
rendered problematic by the epoch-dependence of the UPL: the one-second resonance was not
satisfied at the time life emerged.
The fourth paper also identifies a temporal feature of the system that is worth stating here. The
one-second resonance is not satisfied exactly at the present epoch; the system is about 1.8% short
of closure, and the Moon is receding. On standard tidal models, exact closure will be reached in
roughly 175 to 250 million years. The perfect-eclipse condition — the exact match of lunar and
solar angular sizes at mean distance — was crossed in the opposite direction more than 500
of 5 99
million years ago. Total eclipses have been possible for most of Earth's history, but the exact
match is behind us.
The present epoch therefore sits between two crossings: the perfect eclipse is behind us, and the
resonance is ahead. The only interval in Earth's history when both conditions hold
simultaneously lies in the future, in the few hundred million years after the resonance opens and
before the Moon recedes far enough that eclipses cease. We do not live in that interval. We live
in the one just before it, when the eclipse condition is closing and the resonance condition has
not yet opened.
This does not imply that the resonance caused intelligence, or that the eclipse is a precondition
for mammals. It is a statement about the temporal structure of the system. But it does mean that
the present epoch is the only time in Earth's history when a technological civilization can observe
the resonance approaching exact closure, measure the 1.8% gap, and predict that the system will
eventually satisfy the condition. Observers can only exist at an epoch when the conditions for
their existence are met, and we can only measure the resonance at an epoch when it is
measurably near. That is a selection effect in the strict sense. It is also a specific vantage point,
and the collection records it as one.
The four papers share a common thread, and it is worth stating it plainly. The thread is not a
derivation of the one-second invariant from first principles. The papers do not claim to derive the
value from a deeper theory, and they do not claim to explain why the universe is arranged so that
the invariant holds at every scale. What they claim is narrower: that the invariant is real, that it
spans an enormous range of scales, that the human scale sits at the geometric midpoint between
the quantum and the astrophysical, that the Earth–Moon system is anomalous in a way that bears
on the resonance, and that this anomaly may provide a boundary condition for the chemistry of
life.
The collection owes a debt to the correspondents who have engaged with it. Volynets' kinematic
turning-point analysis corrected an overclaim and clarified the difference between a kinematic
minimum and a dynamical attractor. Sambit Tripathy's Jupiter–Europa calculation, offered as an
external test, gave a result that neither he nor the author expected, and the result is reported in the
fourth paper alongside the systems where it does not hold. Denis Noble's framing of the biology
question — where does a rhythm come from when no genetic instruction specifies it? — is his,
and the extension to planetary chemistry is the collection's. These are acknowledged in the
individual papers, and the acknowledgments are part of the record.
What the reader should look for is not a single unified theory. The collection is not that. It is a set
of related papers that circle around a single observation, each testing it against a different scale,
each reporting what it finds and what it does not. The observation is simple and the consequences
are not. Whether the observation is a coincidence, a selection effect, or a structural feature of the
universe is the question the collection raises and does not fully answer. The answer will come
from the data — from exoplanetary biosignatures, from exomoon statistics, from Europa's ocean,
of 6 99
from the statistics of the satellite population — and the collection is best read as a proposal for
what to look for, not as a claim about what has been found.
The one-second invariant, if it is real, is a feature of a universe whose structure is self-similar
from the quantum to the galactic. The papers in this collection are an exploration of what that
feature might mean. They are offered in that spirit.

Abstract
The Earth–Moon–Sun system satisfies the Universal Particle Law relation to about 2% at the
present epoch, and the present lunar distance is within 1.8% of the value required for exact
closure to one second. This paper develops the planetary-scale case, introduces the celestial
effective action, and asks whether the near-match is a coincidence, a selection effect, or a
structural feature of the dynamics. An independent analysis by Evgeny Volynets has corrected an
earlier claim that the system sits on a dynamically stable plateau; the revised appendix separates
what is observed, what is compared numerically, and what remains an open dynamical question.

direct analogy with the Bohr ground state of hydrogen and leads to a natural definition of
celestial effective actions.

The Earth's rotation is slowing down, and as a direct result, the Moon is slowly drifting away.
Earth's Rotation Slowing: The length of a day is increasing by about 2.3 milliseconds per
century. This is the long-term average rate caused primarily by the Moon's tidal pull. (Note that
this rate can be influenced by other factors; for example, climate change is currently contributing
about 1.33 milliseconds per century).
Moon's Orbit Growing: The Moon is receding from Earth at a rate of about 3.8 centimeters (1.5
inches) per year.
The Tidal Connection
These two phenomena are linked by tidal friction. The Moon's gravity creates tides in Earth's
oceans. As Earth rotates, the tidal bulges are pulled slightly ahead of the Moon, creating friction
that slows Earth's spin.
To conserve angular momentum in the Earth-Moon system, this loss of Earth's rotational speed is
transferred to the Moon, boosting its orbital energy and causing it to spiral outward into a larger
orbit. This recession rate has been precisely measured for decades using the Lunar Laser Ranging
experiment, which bounces lasers off reflectors left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts.
Long-Term Perspective
While these changes are tiny on human timescales, they have significant effects over millions of
years. About 250 million years ago, a day on Earth was roughly 23 hours long. In about 600
million years, the Moon will have drifted so far that total solar eclipses will no longer be
possible.

5. Discussion: Planetary Optimization and the Genesis Analogy
The idea that a planetary system might be precisely tuned for the emergence of life has a rich
history in science fiction. Perhaps the most famous example is Star Trek's "Project Genesis," a
fictional technology designed to reorganize matter at the subatomic level, instantly transforming
a dead celestial body into a thriving, life-sustaining world.
While Genesis is a fantasy of instantaneous terraforming, it highlights a profound cosmological
question: What are the necessary physical conditions for a planetary system to optimize itself for
complex life?
The Universal Particle Law suggests that this optimization is not arbitrary, nor does it require
science-fiction technology. It emerges naturally from the geometric resonance of the Earth-
Moon-Sun system. The Moon’s role is not merely gravitational; it is resonant. It stabilizes Earth's
obliquity, preventing chaotic temperature extremes, and it produces the perfect solar eclipse—a
geometric coincidence where the angular sizes of the Moon and Sun match exactly.
In the framework presented here, the "optimization" of a planet for life is written in the geometry
of the one-second invariant. The near-match between the actual Earth-Moon distance (1.282
light-seconds) and the distance required for exact closure (1.306 light-seconds) is consistent with
a system in a life permitting window. The Moon’s gravitational influence keeps the day length
and tidal forces within a narrow, life permitting window, as Appendix 1 discusses; whether the
window is a dynamical attractor or an empirical near coincidence is an open question.
Where Star Trek imagined an artificial device to create a paradise, the UPL suggests that the
natural dynamics of hierarchical bound systems may already contain the blueprint. The
"Genesis" of a habitable world may be a geometric resonance, not a technological invention.
5.1 The Role of Earth's Obliquity
To understand how this resonance tunes the system, we must look at the role of Earth's obliquity
angle, . The inclusion of in the resonance equation s is physically
justified because the efficiency of tidal coupling depends on the orientation of Earth's rotation
axis relative to the orbital plane (the ecliptic).
1. Geometric Projection of Tidal Forces: The Moon's tidal force on Earth is not applied to a
perfect sphere but to an oblate spheroid (an equatorial bulge). The tidal torque that acts to slow
Earth's rotation and accelerate the Moon's orbit is proportional to the component of the tidal
force that acts along the equatorial plane. As the obliquity changes, the projection of the tidal
force onto the equatorial plane changes, and this projection is described by a factor of (or
related trigonometric functions). Classic analyses of tidal friction, such as those by G.H. Darwin,

A.1 Scope
This appendix reconsiders the relation between the UPL one-second invariant, the present Earth–
Moon–Sun configuration, and the twenty-four-hour day. An earlier draft of this appendix claimed
that the Earth–Moon–Sun system sits on a dynamically stable resonance plateau satisfying
with . An independent analysis by Evgeny Volynets (Harvard Dataverse, doi:10.7910/
DVN/3PVS1E) has shown that in the reduced isolated Earth–Moon model with constant total
angular momentum, the function has a kinematic minimum at km, inside the
current lunar orbit, and that the current system is past this minimum. The distinction between a
kinematic turning point and a dynamically attracting fixed point is essential, and the earlier draft
did not make it.
The revised appendix therefore separates three claims:
1. An empirical observation: at the present epoch, s, and the UPL boundary condition
is satisfied to within about 2%.
2. A numerical comparison: the observed rates of lunar recession and terrestrial spin-down are
consistent with to within the uncertainty of the tidal/climate decomposition, but the
decomposition itself is uncertain.
3. An open dynamical question: whether the present state is attracted toward by the full
tidal evolution. In the isolated model it is not; establishing whether it is in the full three-
dimensional system with solar torque, obliquity evolution, and varying moment of inertia is a
problem for future work.

not that it is at a maximum. The second derivative at the minimum is
confirming that the minimum is a minimum (not a maximum) and that perturbations from it
would grow rather than decay.
The significance of this result for the present appendix is that the kinematic turning point of the
isolated model is not at the present epoch. It occurs at a lunar distance roughly 36% smaller than
the present value, which the Moon passed through on the order of 1.5 Gyr ago (using standard
tidal-recession models). The present epoch is past that turning point, in the direction of
increasing , not at it.
The isolated model is, of course, a simplification: it neglects solar tidal torque, obliquity
evolution, variation of Earth's axial moment of inertia, and the three-dimensional structure of the
angular-momentum transfer. In the full system, the turning point of may be shifted, or may
not have a simple minimum at all. But the isolated model is sufficient to show that the present
epoch is not trivially at a kinematic turning point, and any claim that it is requires the full
analysis of A.6.

lunar tidal torque , solar braking torque , variation of Earth's axial moment of inertia ,
obliquity evolution , and variation of Earth's orbital kinetic energy :
All terms have units of inverse time. A genuine plateau would require this combination to vanish,
and a genuine attractor would require the linearized equation to have with
the full equations of motion including all the terms above.

What the linear analysis does establish is this: if the system were somehow placed at

The Human Scale as a Resonant Node Between the Quantum and
Astrophysical Scales
Ian Beardsley
September 30, 2026
Abstract
We propose that the human scale — the characteristic mass, length, and energy of biological
organisms — is not an arbitrary biological fact but a resonant node between the quantum scale
and the Earth–Moon–Sun scale. Using the Universal Particle Law (UPL), which posits a one-
second resonance governing bound systems from the proton to the galaxy, we construct a human
effective action , where is Planck's constant and is the
Earth–Moon–Sun effective action. With the UPL's one-second timescale, this gives a human
energy scale — on the order of the mechanical work of a heartbeat — and a
characteristic length-to-mass ratio (for ). The geometric means of
particle masses and astrophysical masses bracket the human mass range: ,
, , and . Extending the cascade to the
galactic scale, we identify two additional resonant nodes — the asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU and
Saturn at ~9.5 AU — that complete a scale hierarchy to . We suggest this
hierarchy provides a quantitative framework for astrobiology: the conditions for human-scale
intelligence may be geometrically fixed, and the search for life should target systems with the
same resonant architecture.

sits at the geometric midpoint between the quantum and astrophysical scales.
This is a striking quantitative result: the human mass range is the geometric mean of the quantum
and astrophysical mass scales.

6. Astrobiology Implications
6.1 The resonant architecture
If the human scale is a resonant node between the quantum and astrophysical scales, and if the
Earth–Moon–Sun system is tuned to produce this node, then life requires a planetary system with
specific architectural features:
1. A rocky planet at ~1 AU — where liquid water is stable.
2. An asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU — to deliver water and organics.
3. A gas giant at ~9.5 AU — to shield the inner system.
4. A large moon — to stabilize obliquity and produce a ~24-hour day.
5. A perfect eclipse geometry — , the eclipse ratio.
The UPL predicts these from the Sun's mass, radius, and galactic motion. They are not
independent coincidences; they are resonant nodes of the same one-second law.
6.2 The search strategy
The astrobiology prediction is specific and falsifiable:
Look for exoplanetary systems with an asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU and a gas giant at ~9.5 AU.
These are the systems where the human-scale resonance can emerge.

The Tidal Connection
These two phenomena are linked by tidal friction. The Moon's gravity creates tides in Earth's
oceans. As Earth rotates, the tidal bulges are pulled slightly ahead of the Moon, creating friction
that slows Earth's spin.
To conserve angular momentum in the Earth-Moon system, this loss of Earth's rotational speed is
transferred to the Moon, boosting its orbital energy and causing it to spiral outward into a larger
orbit. This recession rate has been precisely measured for decades using the Lunar Laser Ranging
experiment, which bounces lasers off reflectors left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts.
Long-Term Perspective
While these changes are tiny on human timescales, they have significant effects over millions of
years. About 250 million years ago, a day on Earth was roughly 23 hours long. In about 600
million years, the Moon will have drifted so far that total solar eclipses will no longer be
possible.

7.4 Testability
The framework makes specific predictions:
- The UPL should hold at the human scale with and .
- Exoplanetary systems with an asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU and a gas giant at ~9.5 AU should be

8. Conclusion
We have shown that the human scale emerges as a resonant node between the quantum scale and
the Earth–Moon–Sun scale. The human effective action is the geometric mean of the Planck
constant and the celestial effective action:
With the UPL's one-second resonance, this gives a human energy scale and a
characteristic length-to-mass ratio . The geometric means of particle and
astrophysical masses bracket the human mass range. Extending the cascade to the galactic scale,
we identify the asteroid belt and Saturn as additional resonant nodes.
The human scale is not an arbitrary biological fact. It is the middle rung of a scale hierarchy that
spans from the proton to the galaxy. This suggests a quantitative framework for astrobiology: the
conditions for human-scale intelligence may be geometrically fixed, and the search for life
should target systems with the same resonant architecture.

Appendix: Dimensionless Reformulation of the UPL Hierarchy
A.1 Motivation
A natural objection to the Universal Particle Law (UPL) is that its central result, second,
appears to depend on the human convention of the second. The second, kilogram, meter, and
joule are human units. If the UPL describes a structural resonance, its significance should survive
the removal of human measurement conventions.
This appendix addresses that objection directly. We reformulate the UPL in an -normalized
natural unit system, show that the law collapses to a pure ratio statement, and demonstrate that
the full hierarchy — electron, proton, neutron, Earth–Moon–Sun, human, galaxy — converges to
a single dimensionless coordinate. The resonance survives the removal of SI units.

The 1Hz Resonance: A Physical Basis for the
Master Clock in Biological Systems
Ian Beardsley
Independent Researcher
August 29 - November 2, 2026
Abstract. Denis Noble has argued that the gene centric view of evolution is incomplete,
pointing to the heart as an example of a complex function that lacks a genetic
“instruction” for its rhythm. He asks: where does the heartbeat get its timing if there is
no master clock? This paper proposes that the answer lies not in biology, but in
fundamental physics. The Universal Particle Law (UPL) predicts a universal inertial
resonance at exactly 1 Hz, emerging from the geometry of protons, electrons, and
neutrons. We show that this same resonance governs the EarthMoonSun system and the
structure of the galaxy, implying that the heart’s average rhythm is not an evolutionary
coincidence but a physical alignment with the quantum geometric clock built into all
matter. This provides a concrete, testable mechanism for the “agency” that Noble
attributes to living systems, reframing evolution as a process that occurs within a
universe of resonant attractors.
1. Introduction
The debate between Denis Noble and Richard Dawkins represents a fundamental divide
in evolutionary biology. Dawkins, in The Selfish Gene, posits that the gene is the primary
unit of selection, and that organisms are mere vehicles for gene propagation. Noble
counters that this gene centric view is reductionist and fails to account for the active,
purposeful behaviour of organisms. He argues that there must be some mechanism by
which life guides its own evolution, because complexity cannot be explained by random
mutations alone.
One of Noble’s most compelling examples is the human heart. The heart beats with a
regular rhythm, yet there is no “instruction” in the genome that specifies this rhythm.
There is no master clock. Noble asks: where does the heart get its instructions? The
answer, we propose, lies not in genetics, but in physics. The rhythm of the heart is not
programmed; it is resonant with a fundamental 1Hz (1second) timescale that is inherent
to the structure of matter itself.
2. The Universal Particle Law (UPL)
of 49 99
The Universal Particle Law (Beardsley, 2026) derives from a geometric theory of inertia.
In this view, mass is not an intrinsic property but a resistance to the rotation of a particle’s
velocity vector from the temporal dimension into space. This resistance is quantized by a
normal force:
where is Planck’s constant, is the speed of light, and is a fundamental timescale.
Remarkably, when the UPL is applied to the proton, electron, and neutron, the same value
second emerges:
For the proton, , where is the fine structure constant.
Substituting the measured values of the proton radius ( m) and mass
( kg) gives:
The same calculation for the neutron yields seconds. The electron, with
, gives seconds. Thus, the fundamental particles that constitute all
atoms intrinsically define a timescale of approximately one second.
3. The Heart as a Physical Resonator
The average resting heart rate of a healthy human is approximately 6072 beats per
minute, which corresponds to a frequency of 1.0 to 1.2 Hz, or a period of 0.83 to 1.0
seconds. The UPL predicts that this is not a coincidence. The cardiac pacemaker cells are
composed of protons, neutrons, and electrons—the same particles that collectively define
the 1second resonance.
In the same way that a pendulum’s period is determined by its length and gravity, not by
any “instruction” written into the material, the heart’s rhythm emerges from the collective
electromagnetic and mechanical interactions of its constituent matter. The 1Hz resonance
is a physical attractor: the heart’s natural tendency is to oscillate at this frequency
because it minimizes the inertial resistance required to sustain motion.
This does not mean genes are irrelevant. Genes encode the proteins that form the ion
channels and contractile filaments of heart muscle. But the tempo—the fundamental

4. The Resonance Extends to All Scales
The UPL is scale invariant. The same 1second resonance appears in the EarthMoonSun
system, where the kinetic energy ratio of the Moon and Earth, multiplied by the length of
the day and corrected for obliquity, converges to approximately one second:
This convergence is not a static snapshot. The Moon is receding at 3.8 cm/year, and
Earth's rotation is slowing. The product is currently close to
one second, but it is not at a plateau. As Appendix 1 of the first paper documents, the
present system is past the kinematic minimum of the reduced isolated model, and is
increasing with lunar recession rather than locked at a maximum. The one-second value
is therefore a present-epoch observation, not a dynamically maintained state.
When the UPL is applied to the Sun’s orbit around the galaxy, it predicts two additional
“sweet spots”: an asteroid belt at AU (the volatile delivery zone) and a Saturn
mass planet at AU (the gravitational shield). These are not accidents; they are
resonant nodes fixed by the Sun’s mass, radius, and galactic motion.
5. Implications for Biology and Evolution
The UPL offers a physical foundation for Noble’s systems biology perspective. Living
organisms are not passive vehicles for genes; they are resonant systems that actively tune
to the fundamental clock of matter. This provides a mechanism for the “agency” that
Noble invokes: organisms that align with the 1Hz resonance (and its harmonics, such as
the 24hour circadian cycle) are energetically favoured and have a selective advantage.
Evolution, in this view, is not a purely random process. It unfolds within a landscape of
physical attractors. The complexity of life is guided by these resonances, which act as
boundary conditions on what is possible. The gene is a template, but the tempo—the
rhythm of life—is dictated by the quantum geometry of the cosmos.
This framework makes testable predictions. For example, exoplanet surveys targeting G-
type stars in the solar galactic orbit should find planetary architectures with an Earth-like
planet at 1 AU, an asteroid belt at 2.22.6 AU, and a gas giant at 8.5-10.5 AU. If such

6. Discussion: The Master Clock Resolved
Denis Noble asked: “Where does the heart get its rhythm? There is no master clock.” The
UPL answers: the master clock is inside every proton, neutron, and electron. It is not a
biological instruction, but a physical resonance. The heart beats at approximately 1 Hz
because that is the natural inertial frequency of the matter it is made of, and because
evolution has selected organisms that are energetically aligned with this fundamental
timescale.
This does not reduce biology to physics—it enriches it. It shows that life is not an
accidental byproduct of random chemistry, but a natural expression of a universe whose
structure is self-similar from the quantum to the galactic scale. The same law that builds
protons also builds solar systems, and it does so in a way that maximizes the chances for
stable, complex, intelligent life.
7. Conclusion
We have shown that the Universal Particle Law provides a direct, physical answer to
Noble’s critique of the gene centric view. The 1second resonance is not a human
convention; it is a fundamental eigenvalue of matter that emerges from quantum
chromodynamics and propagates through hierarchical scales to planetary and galactic
systems. The heart’s rhythm, the 24hour day, the asteroid belt, and Saturn’s orbit are all
nodes of the same cosmic clock.
Life is not guided by random mutations alone; it is guided by the resonant structure of the
universe. The master clock does not exist in the genome—it exists in the geometry of
spacetime and the particles that inhabit it. We are not merely observers of this cosmic
order; we are its resonant expression.

The Large-Moon Condition: Anomalous Satellite Mass and the Resonance
Architecture of Habitable Worlds
Ian Beardsley
Independent Researcher
November 2, 2026
Abstract
The Moon is anomalously massive for a terrestrial planet. Its mass ratio to Earth,
, exceeds that of any other satellite–planet pair in the Solar System apart
from the Pluto–Charon binary. This paper examines three independent lines of evidence that
converge on as a parameter of astrobiological significance.
First, the large-moon hypothesis: a satellite of lunar mass stabilizes a planet's obliquity against
secular and chaotic variation, and drives tidal forcing that may contribute to prebiotic chemistry.
The hypothesis is a window rather than a threshold — Waltham (2006) shows that a somewhat
more massive Moon would have destabilized Earth's obliquity — and its formation mechanism,
the giant impact, faces unresolved isotopic and dynamical problems that are reviewed here.
Second, the celestial resonance: the Earth–Moon–Sun system satisfies a Bohr-analogue action
condition to about 1%, and a Universal Particle Law (UPL) relation to about 2% at the present
epoch. Reducing the Bohr analogue to classical form eliminates every quantum symbol and
yields , where . This relation scales as and is Earth-
specific: applied uniformly to the Solar System's large satellites it returns 1.13 s for the Earth–
Moon system, 0.26 s for Saturn–Titan, 0.29 s for Neptune–Triton, and s for Jupiter–
Europa.
Third, the exoplanetary context: formation and survival constraints suggest that Earth-like moon
systems are uncommon, with Elser et al. (2011) estimating the probability of a terrestrial planet
acquiring a lunar-mass satellite at roughly 13%, and Brasser et al. (2013) finding that only about
14% of such systems evolve to an Earth-like configuration, giving a combined estimate of the
order of 2%.
The paper distinguishes three claims. The weak claim is that the UPL relation holds empirically
at the present epoch. The strong claim — that abiogenesis requires the one-second resonance —
is rendered problematic by the epoch-dependence of the UPL: because the Moon was closer in
the past, the one-second value was not satisfied at the time of abiogenesis. This paper therefore
advances a third position, the filter hypothesis: the resonance condition acts as a selection effect
on planetary architecture, favoring systems whose satellite-to-planet mass ratios are

hypothesis is time-independent, because it depends on the Moon's mass ratio rather than its
orbital radius.
The paper also identifies a temporal feature of the system. The present epoch is approximately
1.8% short of exact resonance closure, and the Moon is receding. Exact closure will be reached
in roughly 175 to 250 million years. The perfect-eclipse condition — the exact match of lunar
and solar angular sizes — was crossed in the opposite direction more than 500 million years ago.
The present epoch therefore sits between the two crossings: the perfect eclipse is behind us, and
the resonance is ahead. We live in the interval just before the resonance opens, which is the only
time in Earth's history when a technological civilization can observe the resonance approaching
exact closure.
Three tests of the filter hypothesis are proposed: exomoon statistics around habitable-zone
planets; obliquity stability as a proxy in the absence of detectable moons; and the Waltham
window, which predicts that planets with satellites substantially more massive than the Moon's
should be less habitable, not more. None of these tests is currently feasible; all are within reach
of planned instrumentation.
What the paper does not claim is stated explicitly. It does not claim that the Moon is necessary
for life, that the canonical giant impact model is correct, or that the resonance causes the large-
moon condition to be selected. It claims that three independent lines of evidence point at the
same parameter, that the correlation is worth testing, and that the test is falsifiable.
1. Introduction: The Anomalous Moon
1.1 The observation
Among the terrestrial planets, Earth's satellite is anomalous. Mercury and Venus have no
satellites. Mars has two small bodies, Phobos and Deimos, whose combined mass is less than
of Mars's. Earth, alone among the terrestrial planets, has a satellite massive enough to exert
a significant torque on its spin axis and to raise substantial ocean tides.
The mass ratio is
and the radius ratio is . The Moon is roughly a quarter of Earth's diameter and
about one-eightieth of its mass. Among the planets, only the Pluto–Charon system has a
comparable satellite-to-planet ratio, and that system is more properly described as a binary than
as a planet–moon pair.

This is an empirical fact, and it is the starting point for everything that follows. The question is
whether it matters — whether the Moon's anomalous mass is a curiosity about Earth's history, or
whether it is a condition that bears on the habitability of the planet.
1.2 Why the question is not trivial
There are two ways to regard the Moon's mass. The first is that it is an accident of Earth's
particular accretion history — a consequence of a specific impact at a specific time — with no
implications beyond the fact that Earth has a companion. On this reading, the Moon is a feature
of Earth's biography, not a condition for its habitability.
The second is that a satellite of lunar mass performs dynamical functions — stabilizing obliquity,
driving tides — that are plausibly relevant to the long-term persistence of complex life. On this
reading, the Moon is part of the reason Earth is habitable, not merely part of its history.
The two readings are not mutually exclusive. The Moon can be an accident of history and have
habitability consequences. But they place different weight on the observation, and they make
different predictions about which other planets should host complex life. The first predicts that
habitability is largely independent of satellite mass; the second predicts that it is not.
This paper does not settle the question. It argues that the question is well posed, that three
independent lines of evidence converge on as a parameter of significance, and that the
convergence is testable.
1.3 The structure of the argument
The argument proceeds in three parts.
Part I: The large-moon hypothesis (§2–3). A satellite of lunar mass stabilizes a planet's obliquity
against secular and chaotic variation and drives tidal forcing that may contribute to prebiotic
chemistry. The hypothesis is more constrained than it is often presented — it is a window rather
than a threshold — and its formation mechanism, the giant impact, faces unresolved problems.
Part II: The celestial resonance (§4–6). The Earth–Moon–Sun system satisfies a Bohr-analogue
action condition to about 1%, and a Universal Particle Law relation to about 2% at the present
epoch. Both conditions reduce to numerical statements about , and neither survives when
applied uniformly to the Solar System's other large satellites. Earth is the only system where the
resonance condition and the large-moon condition coincide.
Part III: The filter hypothesis (§7–8). The convergence of the two lines of evidence is stated as a
hypothesis: that the resonance condition may act as a selection effect on planetary architecture,
favouring systems whose mass ratios are simultaneously compatible with the resonance and with
q

of 56 99
long-term obliquity stability. The hypothesis is distinguished from the weak and strong claims
already in the literature, and three tests are proposed.
Section 9 reports three tests that failed, and explains why the failures matter for the credibility of
the result that survives. Section 10 places the argument in the exoplanetary context. Section 11
states what is established and what is not.
1.4 The epistemic standard
The framework this paper examines has a history of overclaim. An earlier draft of the one-second
invariant paper claimed that the Earth–Moon–Sun system sits on a dynamically stable resonance
plateau; an independent analysis by Volynets (2026) showed that in the reduced isolated model
the relevant function has a kinematic minimum, not an attractor, and that the present system is
past that minimum. The claim was withdrawn and the revised paper distinguishes three things:
what is observed, what is compared numerically, and what remains an open dynamical question.
This paper adopts the same standard. Throughout, claims are marked as established, supported,
or hypothesis. Numerical coincidences are reported as coincidences, not as mechanisms. Tests
that failed are reported alongside tests that passed. The argument is at its strongest when it
reports what it can defend and says plainly what it cannot.
2. The Large-Moon Hypothesis
2.1 Obliquity stabilisation
A planet's obliquity — the tilt of its spin axis relative to its orbital plane — is subject to secular
variation driven by gravitational torques from the Sun and from neighbouring planets. For a
planet with no massive satellite, these torques can drive the obliquity through large excursions,
and in some cases into chaos.
The classic analysis is Laskar and colleagues (1993), who showed that without the Moon, Earth's
obliquity would vary chaotically over a range of roughly to on timescales of tens of
millions of years. With the Moon, the obliquity is confined to a narrow band — roughly to
over the last several million years, with longer-term variation of a few degrees around the
present value.
The climatic consequence is significant. Obliquity sets the amplitude and distribution of seasonal
insolation. A planet with a stable, moderate obliquity has predictable seasons and a stable climate
over geological time. A planet with a wildly varying obliquity may alternate between states in
which its poles or its equator receive most of the insolation, with correspondingly extreme
climatic shifts.

The argument for habitability is that complex life requires climatic stability over hundreds of
millions of years, and obliquity stabilization is a plausible enabling condition for such stability.
This is a plausible argument, not a demonstrated one: the fossil record shows that life has
persisted through substantial climatic variation, and the threshold of obliquity variation beyond
which complex life cannot persist is not known.
2.2 Tidal forcing
A second mechanism is tidal. The Moon raises tides in Earth's oceans, and the intertidal zone —
periodically flooded and exposed — is one of the environments proposed for the origin of life.
The argument is that cyclic wet–dry conditions concentrate organic molecules and drive
condensation and polymerization reactions that would not occur in a static environment.
This argument is more speculative than the obliquity argument, because the relevant prebiotic
chemistry is not established. It is a plausible mechanism, not a demonstrated one. But it is worth
noting that the tidal amplitude depends on the satellite's mass and distance, and a satellite
substantially less massive than the Moon would produce correspondingly weaker tides.
2.3 The Waltham window
The large-moon hypothesis is often stated as a threshold: larger satellites are better. This is not
correct. Waltham (2006) showed that when tidal dissipation of the planet's spin is included in the
analysis, a sufficiently massive satellite can destabilize obliquity rather than stabilize it. The
mechanism is that the satellite's tidal torque changes the precession frequency of the planet's spin
axis, and if the precession frequency approaches a resonance with the orbital precession, the
obliquity can be driven to large values.
In Waltham's analysis, the Moon lies close to the upper limit of satellite mass compatible with
axial stability. A somewhat more massive Moon would have driven Earth's obliquity into the
unstable regime. The large-moon hypothesis is therefore a window rather than a threshold: the
satellite must be massive enough to stabilize the obliquity against solar torques, but not so
massive that its own tidal torque destabilizes it.
This is an important refinement, and it has a specific consequence for the filter hypothesis in §7.
If the large-moon condition is a window, then the prediction is not "more massive moons are
better" but "moons in a specific mass range are compatible with stability." A planet with a
satellite substantially more massive than the Moon's should be less habitable, not more. This is a
falsifiable prediction, and it distinguishes the window hypothesis from a naive threshold reading.
2.4 What the hypothesis does and does not claim
The large-moon hypothesis, in the form defended here, claims the following:
of 58 99
Established. A satellite of lunar mass stabilizes Earth's obliquity against chaotic variation, and
drives ocean tides. Both effects are well-documented.
Supported. Obliquity stability is plausibly relevant to the long-term persistence of complex life.
This is a plausible inference, not a demonstrated requirement.
Hypothesis. A satellite of lunar mass is a significant, perhaps necessary, condition for a planet to
be a successful host of complex life. This is the claim the paper advances, and it is the claim the
filter hypothesis in §7 makes testable.
It does not claim that the Moon is necessary for life. A planet without a large moon might be
habitable by other routes — tidal heating from a close orbit, obliquity stabilization by a different
mechanism, or simply a climate system robust to obliquity variation. The hypothesis is that large
moons enhance the probability of long-term habitability, not that they are required.
3. The Origin of the Moon: Consensus and Its Problems
3.1 Why the origin matters for the argument
Section 2 established that the Moon's mass is anomalous and that its anomalous mass is the
parameter on which the habitability argument and the resonance argument both depend. Neither
argument requires a particular origin story: the empirical fact is that , and that fact
stands regardless of how the Moon formed.
But the frequency of large-moon systems — and therefore the strength of the filter hypothesis in
§7 — does depend on the origin. If lunar-mass satellites arise readily from ordinary planet
formation, then Earth-like moon systems are common and the filter selects from a large
population. If they require a rare dynamical event, then the population is small and the filter is
more restrictive. The origin question therefore bears directly on the quantitative predictions of
the hypothesis, even though it does not bear on the qualitative observation.
3.2 The canonical model and what it explains
The giant impact hypothesis proposes that a Mars-sized body, conventionally called Theia, struck
the proto-Earth late in its accretion, and that the Moon formed from the ejected debris. The
hypothesis was proposed independently by Hartmann and Davis (1975) and by Cameron and
Ward (1976), and the canonical version was developed through smoothed-particle hydrodynamic
simulations by Canup and colleagues in the 2000s (Canup & Asphaug 2001; Canup 2004).
The model explains several features that competing hypotheses do not:
- Angular momentum. The Earth–Moon system has substantially more angular momentum per
unit mass than the other terrestrial planets. A grazing impact is a natural source.
q ≈ 0.0123
of 59 99
- The Moon's small core. The Moon's core is roughly 1–2% of its mass, against ~32% for Earth.
Debris ejected from the impact is drawn preferentially from the silicate mantles of both bodies,
so a low-iron Moon is a natural outcome.
- The Moon's bulk composition. The Moon is broadly chondritic in its refractory element ratios,
consistent with derivation from terrestrial mantle material rather than from a compositionally
distinct body.
- Earth's obliquity. The present tilt is consistent with the geometry of a late, oblique impact.
For two decades the canonical model was the consensus, and it remains the reference against
which alternatives are measured. The problems below are problems with the canonical version,
not evidence that no impact occurred.
3.3 Problem 1: the isotopic similarity
The most serious difficulty is isotopic. Since the 2000s, high-precision measurements have
shown that Earth and the Moon are indistinguishable in their oxygen, titanium, silicon, and
tungsten isotopic compositions, to within a few parts per million (oxygen: Young et al. 2016;
titanium: Zhang et al. 2012; tungsten: Touboul et al. 2007; Kruijer et al. 2015; the oxygen result
was tightened substantially by Hosono et al. 2019).
This is a problem because the canonical impact ejects material drawn from both bodies, with the
Moon forming predominantly from the impactor's mantle. If Theia formed elsewhere in the solar
nebula, it should carry a distinct isotopic signature — the isotopic variability among solar system
bodies is well documented, and Mars, Vesta, and the various chondrite groups are all measurably
distinct from Earth. The observed Earth–Moon identity therefore requires either that Theia
happened to be isotopically identical to Earth, which is a coincidence of low probability, or that
the impactor and the proto-Earth were thoroughly mixed before the Moon condensed.
The first option is disfavoured on general grounds: it replaces one coincidence with another and
offers no reason why Theia should resemble Earth more closely than Mars or Vesta do. The
second option is the more productive line, and it has generated the principal revisions to the
model (§3.7).
3.4 Problem 2: volatile depletion
A related but distinct line of evidence concerns the Moon's volatile elements. The Moon is
depleted in moderately volatile elements — potassium, zinc, sodium — relative to Earth, and the
depletion pattern is consistent with loss during a high-temperature episode.
The zinc isotope system is particularly informative: the Moon's zinc is isotopically heavier than
Earth's, in a pattern consistent with evaporative loss of light isotopes (Paniello et al. 2012).
Potassium isotopes show a similar signature (Wang & Jacobsen 2016). These observations
indicate that the Moon-forming material experienced substantial heating and vapour loss, which

is consistent with a high-energy impact but in some tension with the canonical model's relatively
modest energy budget.
This problem cuts differently from the isotopic problem: it points toward a higher-energy event,
whereas the isotopic problem points toward more thorough mixing. Both lines of evidence
favour the higher-energy variants discussed in §3.7.
3.5 Problem 3: angular momentum
The Earth–Moon system's angular momentum is kg m² s⁻¹, corresponding to a
dimensionless spin parameter of about 0.39. The canonical impact, with a Mars-
mass impactor at the most probable impact angle, produces somewhat less than the observed
value. Reproducing the observed angular momentum requires either a larger impactor, a higher
impact velocity, or a more oblique geometry than the canonical parameters assume.
The tension is not severe — the canonical model can be tuned to match the angular momentum
— but the required tuning reduces the model's predictive power, and it is one motivation for the
higher-energy variants.
3.6 Problem 4: dynamical probability
The impact geometry required by the canonical model is specific. The impactor must be massive
enough to eject a lunar-mass debris disk, and the impact must be oblique enough to impart the
observed angular momentum without disrupting the proto-Earth entirely. Estimates of the
fraction of terrestrial planet formation histories that produce such an event vary, but they are not
large.
This is the most directly relevant problem for the present argument, because it is the one that
determines the frequency of large-moon systems. If the required impact is a 1-in-10 event, large-
moon systems are common enough that the filter hypothesis draws from a substantial population.
If it is a 1-in-1000 event, they are rare, and the filter is far more restrictive.
3.7 Proposed resolutions
Three families of resolution have been developed in response to the isotopic problem.
Equilibration through a silicate vapour atmosphere. Pahlevan and Stevenson (2007) proposed
that the post-impact Earth was surrounded by a hot silicate vapour atmosphere through which the
impactor's material and the proto-Earth's material exchanged isotopes before the Moon
condensed. The mechanism is physically plausible and has been developed in subsequent work.
Its difficulty is that it requires the exchange to be efficient enough to homogenize oxygen,
titanium, and tungsten simultaneously, which places constraints on the temperature and duration
of the vapour phase.

Hosono et al. (2019) propose a different resolution: a large solid impactor struck a magma-
ocean-covered proto-Earth, so that the ejected material was drawn primarily from the terrestrial
magma ocean rather than from the impactor. This differs from the vapour-equilibration model of
Pahlevan and Stevenson (2007), in which isotopic exchange occurs between impactor material
and the proto-Earth's mantle through a hot extended vapour atmosphere before the Moon
condenses.
The synestia model. Lock and Stewart (2017, 2018) proposed that sufficiently high-energy, high-
angular-momentum impacts produce a rotating, vapourised structure — a "synestia" — in which
the distinction between the impactor and the target is erased before the Moon forms. The Moon
then condenses from the vapour in the outer regions of the structure. The model reproduces the
isotopic identity naturally, and it is consistent with the volatile depletion signature. Its cost is that
it requires the impact to be substantially more energetic than the canonical model assumes, with
correspondingly lower dynamical probability.
High-angular-momentum impacts with evection resonance. Ćuk and Stewart (2012) and Canup
(2012) independently proposed that a high-angular-momentum impact, followed by passage
through the evection resonance with the Sun, could remove angular momentum from the Earth–
Moon system while preserving the isotopic identity of the Moon. In this scenario the Moon
forms from a disk derived largely from Earth's mantle, and the present angular momentum is the
residue after resonance-driven loss. The model has the advantage of explaining the isotopic
similarity without requiring an unusually energetic impact; its difficulty is that the resonance
passage must occur at a specific time and with specific parameters.
None of these resolutions is established. The synestia and evection-resonance models both
require the impact to be higher-energy than the canonical model, which reduces the estimated
frequency of such events. The equilibration model does not require higher energy but requires
efficient mixing.
3.8 The alternatives and why they are worse
Three pre-impact hypotheses are worth stating, because the fact that the giant impact is
problematic does not mean an alternative is correct.
Capture. The Moon formed elsewhere and was captured. This fails on dynamical grounds —
capture requires dissipation of the relative velocity, and no plausible mechanism exists for a body
of lunar mass — and on isotopic grounds, since a captured body would carry a distinct signature.
Fission. The Moon split off from a rapidly rotating Earth. This fails on angular momentum: a
fissioning Earth would need to rotate at or near breakup, and no mechanism has been identified
that would spin it to that state and then remove the excess angular momentum. It also fails on the
of 62 99
isotopic composition of the Moon, which is not consistent with derivation from a small fraction
of Earth's mantle alone.
Co-accretion. Earth and Moon accreted together from the same region of the disk. This fails on
mass: co-accretion cannot produce a body of lunar mass without also producing a much larger
population of intermediate bodies, which is not observed. It also fails to explain the Moon's low
iron content.
The giant impact is therefore the least problematic of the available hypotheses, even in its
contested form. The correct summary is that an impact of some kind is well supported, the
canonical parameters are under pressure, and the higher-energy variants are the most promising
current direction.
3.9 What this means for the filter hypothesis
Three statements can be made with confidence, and one cannot.
Established. The Moon is anomalously massive. The giant impact hypothesis is the best-
supported origin, and the alternatives are substantially less viable. The canonical parameters face
serious isotopic and volatile-element problems, and the higher-energy variants are the most likely
resolution.
Not established. The frequency of lunar-mass satellite formation. The dynamical probability of
the required impact is uncertain by at least an order of magnitude, and the higher-energy variants
reduce it further. Any quantitative estimate of how common Earth-like moon systems are should
carry a correspondingly large uncertainty.
For the filter hypothesis in §7, this means the qualitative claim — that the resonance condition
may select for satellite-to-planet mass ratios compatible with long-term habitability — is
unaffected, because it depends only on the empirical value of . The quantitative prediction —
how many such systems should exist — cannot be made with confidence until the formation
frequency is better constrained. The hypothesis should therefore be stated qualitatively, and the
quantitative prediction deferred.

This relation is numerically striking, but it is important to be clear about its status. The effective
action is fixed by the Bohr-analogue condition, not by the kinetic-energy relation. The
kinetic-energy relation is a consequence of the numerical coincidence that
happens to be close to . It is not an independent derivation, and it does not establish a

4.4 What the one-second value does and does not mean
The UPL relation returns s at the present epoch. The question is what this value
means.
It does not mean that one second is a fundamental constant. The second is a human unit, derived
from Earth's rotation and base-60 numeration. The framework does not claim that the universe is
calibrated in seconds.
What the relation does claim is narrower: that a ratio of the form
evaluates to approximately one second for the Earth–Moon–Sun system. Whether this is
coincidence, selection, or structure is the open question that the framework raises and does not
settle. The three interpretations are distinguished in §8.
The dimensionless reformulation in Appendix A shows that the ratio survives the removal of SI
units: in -normalized natural units, the UPL collapses to , and every scale
converges to . The value s is the human projection of that dimensionless ratio.
This is what makes the relation structural rather than metrological, and it is worth stating
explicitly because the dimensional objection is the first one a careful reader will raise.

The ordering tracks almost exactly, as the reduction predicts. Earth is the only system in the

This result has two implications. First, the Bohr analogue is Earth-specific; it does not describe a

disagree by four orders of magnitude for Europa. They are not two expressions of one law.
5.4 What the reduction means for the hypothesis
The reduction points somewhere useful, but not where the "Bohr resonance" framing suggests.
The analogue works for Earth because Earth has an unusually massive moon — , the

independent explanation in the giant impact (§3), and an independent consequence in obliquity
stabilization (§2). The chain is:
giant impact → large Moon → large → Bohr analogue lands near 1 s → (possibly) habitability.

6.3 The threshold result
The most robust pattern in the satellite data is not a harmonic series but a threshold. Sorting
every major moon by mass, the kinetic form's output is sharply bimodal:

than a gradient, and the step coincides with a real, well-documented gap in the satellite

The critical-mass statement is defensible: the kinetic-energy form returns order-one seconds for
the seven large satellites and sub-second values for every smaller one. This is a claim that could
have failed — if any small moon had returned a value near 1 s, the threshold claim would have

6.4 A caveat on the threshold
The threshold result is a test the formula passed, but it is not a prediction of the formula. The
seven large regular satellites are exactly the class planetary scientists already distinguish from the
small-body population. The reframing must therefore be stated as: the formula is sensitive to a
mass threshold that coincides with the known large/small dichotomy. That is interesting — it
means the formula tracks a real physical class — but it is not a new prediction, and a referee will
say so immediately if the paper does not say it first.
The non-trivial version of the claim is narrower: among systems that cross the threshold, the ones
that land near 1 s are the ones astrobiologically interesting (Europa, the Moon). That is testable
in a way the harmonic claim is not.
6.5 Uranus as a domain-of-validity case
The Uranian system cannot be treated by the kinetic form. Its obliquity of exceeds , so
the factor — introduced as a tidal-coupling projection for small-to-moderate obliquity —
changes sign, and the formula returns negative values for every Uranian moon.
This is a domain-of-validity limit, not a test the system fails. The factor was calibrated for
the Earth–Moon and Jupiter–Europa geometries; it was never designed for a planet lying on its
side. Independently, Uranus has no moon above the kg threshold (Titania, the largest, is
kg), so even a repaired obliquity factor would place its moons in the small- group.
Uranus is therefore outside the formula's reach for two separate reasons, and neither is evidence
against the architecture. It is worth noting that the Uranian system is physically distinct: its
obliquity is the result of a likely giant impact, and its moons formed or were captured in the post-
impact equatorial plane. The tidal dynamics of that system are genuinely different from the
Earth–Moon or Jupiter–Europa systems, and the heuristic was never built to capture them.
7. The Filter Hypothesis
7.1 The convergence
Sections 2 and 5 identified two independent pointers to the same parameter . The large-moon
hypothesis identifies as the variable that controls obliquity stability and tidal forcing. The Bohr
analogue identifies as the variable that controls whether the celestial resonance condition is
satisfied. Neither implies the other, and neither is a mechanism. But both point at the same
quantity.
The convergence is the basis for the hypothesis advanced in this section.

7.2 Three claims
The paper distinguishes three claims of increasing strength.
The weak claim (boundary condition). The UPL relation holds empirically at the present epoch:
s, within about 2% of unity. This is an observation about the present configuration. It
does not assert a mechanism, and it does not assert that the relation was satisfied in the past or
will be in the future.
The strong claim (causal requirement), and its epoch-dependence problem. The abiogenesis
paper (Beardsley 2026b) advanced the hypothesis that abiogenesis requires the one-second
resonance. However, the UPL relation depends on the Moon's orbital radius, , and has
increased over geological time. At the time of abiogenesis, the Moon was at roughly 60% of its
present distance, meaning would have been approximately 0.6 seconds, not 1 second.
Therefore, the strong claim cannot be strictly correct: life emerged at an epoch when the
resonance was not satisfied. The strong claim is superseded by the filter hypothesis.
The filter hypothesis (selection effect). The resonance is neither a boundary condition on
chemistry nor a requirement for abiogenesis, but a selection effect on planetary architecture.
Systems that satisfy the resonance at some point in their history are more likely to have the
stable, long-lived environment in which complex life can persist. The filter does not act on
chemistry; it acts on the population of planetary systems, favoring those whose mass ratios are
simultaneously compatible with the resonance and with long-term obliquity stability.
The filter hypothesis is weaker than the strong claim, because it does not require a mechanism by
which the resonance acts on chemistry. It is stronger than the weak claim, because it makes a
prediction about which systems should host complex life, rather than merely noting a numerical
coincidence on Earth.
7.3 The logic of the filter
The filter hypothesis rests on three premises, each of which is independently supported.
Premise 1. A satellite of lunar mass stabilizes a planet's obliquity against chaotic variation, and a
satellite substantially more massive destabilizes it. This is the Waltham window (§2.3), and it is
supported by dynamical modeling.
Premise 2. Obliquity stability is plausibly relevant to the long-term persistence of complex life.
This is a plausible inference, not a demonstrated requirement, but it is widely accepted.
Premise 3. The celestial resonance condition scales as , so it is satisfied only for satellite-to-
planet mass ratios in a narrow range. This is the reduction in §5, and it is a mathematical
consequence of the Bohr analogue.

The conclusion is that the range of compatible with the resonance is also, approximately, the
range compatible with obliquity stability. Systems in that range have both a stable climate and a
satisfied resonance condition; systems outside it have neither. If both conditions are relevant to
habitability, the population of habitable planets is filtered toward the mass ratios that satisfy both.
The logic is probabilistic, not deterministic. The filter does not say that only resonant systems
can host life; it says that resonant systems are more likely to. A planet without a large moon
might be habitable by another route — tidal heating, a different obliquity-stabilization
mechanism, a robust climate system. The filter says that such planets are less likely, not that they
are impossible.
7.4 What the filter does not claim
It does not claim that the Moon is necessary for life. A planet without a large moon might be
habitable by other routes.
It does not claim that the giant impact hypothesis is correct in its canonical form. The argument
depends only on the empirical fact that the Moon is massive, not on the mechanism by which it
became so.
It does not claim that the UPL resonance causes the large-moon condition to be selected. The two
arguments point at the same parameter , but whether the resonance is causally involved in the
selection, or whether both are consequences of some third factor, is not established. The
hypothesis is that the correlation is worth testing, not that it has been explained.
It does not claim that the filter is the only selection effect on habitability. Other factors — stellar
type, orbital architecture, atmospheric composition, magnetic field — are surely relevant. The
filter is one effect among many.
7.5 Why state it as a hypothesis
The filter hypothesis is stated as a hypothesis for three reasons.
The mechanism is not specified. The framework establishes that the resonance condition holds,
and that it scales as . It does not establish a mechanism by which the resonance acts on
planetary architecture. The filter is a description of a correlation, not an explanation of it.
Alternative explanations are not ruled out. The correlation between and habitability could be a
selection effect (we observe a large moon because large moons are required for life), a
coincidence (Earth happens to have both), or a structure (there is a deeper reason why both hold).
The filter hypothesis is one of these alternatives, and it has not been distinguished from the
others.

The empirical evidence is not yet decisive. The Solar System provides one data point — Earth —
and the satellite data show that the resonance is Earth-specific. A sample of one cannot
distinguish a selection effect from a coincidence.
7.6 The relation to the abiogenesis paper
The abiogenesis paper advances the weak and strong claims. The filter hypothesis is a third
position, and it is worth stating explicitly how it relates to the other two.
The weak claim is the empirical observation: the Earth–Moon–Sun system satisfies the UPL
relation to about 2% at the present epoch. The filter hypothesis accepts this claim and adds that
the coincidence may reflect a selection effect on planetary architecture.
The strong claim is the causal requirement: abiogenesis requires the resonance. The filter
hypothesis is weaker than this, because it does not require a mechanism. A planet could satisfy
the resonance and still be sterile; the filter says only that such a planet is more likely to be
habitable than one that does not.
The filter hypothesis is therefore a middle position. It is more specific than the weak claim,
because it makes a prediction about which systems should host complex life. It is less demanding
than the strong claim, because it does not require the resonance to act on chemistry.
It is important to state that the filter hypothesis supersedes the strong claim of the earlier
abiogenesis paper. Because the one-second value is epoch-dependent—and was not satisfied at
the time of abiogenesis—the strong claim (that abiogenesis requires the resonance) cannot be
maintained. The filter hypothesis is not vulnerable to this temporal problem, because it depends
only on the satellite-to-planet mass ratio, which is time-independent. The Moon's mass, unlike its
orbital radius, has not changed.
7.7 The epoch just before the resonance
There is a temporal feature of the Earth–Moon system that is worth stating explicitly, because it
clarifies the relationship between the resonance, the present epoch, and the emergence of
intelligent life.
The UPL one-second relation is not satisfied exactly at the present epoch. The system is within
about 1.8% of exact closure: the actual lunar distance is 1.282 light-seconds, while the distance
required for s is 1.306 light-seconds. Because the Moon is receding, the system is
approaching the resonance, not receding from it. On standard tidal models, the Moon will cross
the exact-closure distance in roughly 175 to 250 million years.

The geological and fossil records place the emergence of Homo sapiens at roughly 0.3 million
years ago. The entire history of our species is therefore a tiny fraction of the time remaining
before the resonance closes.
This leads to a specific, factual observation: we exist just before the resonance opens, not at the
moment it is satisfied. The present epoch is the window in which a technological civilization can
measure the resonance at a distance of 1.8% from closure, compute the tidal recession, and
predict that the system will eventually satisfy the condition exactly.
This observation does not require a mechanism, and it does not claim that the resonance caused
intelligence. It is a statement about the temporal structure of the system. However, it reframes the
significance of the present-day near-match. If intelligent life had emerged 500 million years ago,
the Moon would have been too close for the one-second resonance to be near closure, and the
numerical coincidence we observe today would not have been present to measure. If intelligent
life emerges 500 million years from now, the resonance will have been crossed, and the Moon
will be receding away from the condition. We happen to live in the specific geological window
where the system is approaching the resonance, and where the mathematics of the system can be
observed at near-closure.
This is a selection effect in the strict sense: observers must exist at an epoch when the conditions
for their existence are met, and we can only measure the resonance at an epoch when the
resonance is measurably close. But it is a narrow window. The present epoch sits just before the
resonance opens, and this is the only time in Earth's history when the Moon is simultaneously
large enough for obliquity stability, close enough for the resonance to be measurably near, and
approaching exact closure.
The relationship between the resonance and the perfect-eclipse condition is worth stating
explicitly, because both depend on the same variable and both have been proposed as
astrobiologically relevant. The perfect-eclipse condition — the lunar and solar angular sizes
matching at mean distance — was crossed more than 500 million years ago on the tidal
rhythmite record. Total solar eclipses have been possible for most of Earth's history, but the exact
match of angular sizes is behind us: the Moon now appears slightly smaller than the Sun at mean
distance, and total eclipses occur only because the lunar orbit is eccentric and the Moon is closer
at perigee.
The one-second resonance, by contrast, has not yet been crossed. It will be reached in roughly
175 to 250 million years. The present epoch therefore sits between the two crossings: the perfect
eclipse is behind us, and the resonance is ahead.
This has a specific consequence. In the future, there will be a period of a few hundred million
years during which both conditions are satisfied simultaneously — the resonance will have
opened, and total eclipses will still occur — before the Moon recedes far enough that eclipses
cease. That future overlap is the only interval in Earth's history when both conditions hold at
of 75 99
once. We do not live in it. We live in the interval just before it, when the eclipse condition is
closing and the resonance condition has not yet opened.
7.8 The recurrence of one second
The preceding sections have introduced four distinct constructions that each return a value close
to one second for the Earth–Moon–Sun system. It is worth stating explicitly what each of them
is, because they are not four independent coincidences, and they should not be presented as such.
The four constructions are:

the UPL applied to the Earth–Moon–Sun system, which agrees with one second to about 2% at
the present epoch;
the numerical proximity of the celestial effective action to Earth's orbital kinetic energy, which
agrees to about 6%;
the kinetic-energy form, which returns roughly 1.15 s for the Earth–Moon system with mean
orbital velocities, and 0.99 s with aphelion/perihelion values.
These four values are not equal, and they are not independent. Two of them are epoch-
independent; two are epoch-dependent.

, and the value that results is a choice of how to set the scale, not an empirical

The observation, then, is not that four constructions independently return one second. It is that
two epoch-independent constructions give exactly or approximately one second, and that we
happen to live at the epoch where the two epoch-dependent constructions also give
approximately one second. The four-way convergence is a property of the present epoch, not of
the framework.
This connects directly to the temporal structure described in §7.7. The reason we live at the
epoch where the convergence occurs is a selection effect: observers must exist at an epoch when
the conditions for their existence are met, and those conditions include the Moon at
approximately its present distance. As §7.7 notes, we live in the window just before the
resonance opens — just before the epoch-dependent constructions cross the value set by the
epoch-independent ones. The convergence of all four constructions on one second is a specific
vantage point, and the framework records it as one.
There is a potential confusion here that is worth resolving. The Universal Particle Law posits
as a characteristic interval set by the quantization of temporal momentum. In that sense, is an
eigenvalue of matter, not a human convention: it is the interval over which the normal force is
defined, and the fact that the proton, neutron, and electron independently return the same value is
evidence that the eigenvalue is real.
However, the numerical value of the eigenvalue in seconds is a projection. In -normalized
natural units, the ratio is approximately . The value "one second" is what that ratio
looks like when measured with a clock built by organisms of a particular size. The reason it
looks like one second is not that the universe is calibrated in seconds, but that the resonance sits
at the human scale.
The four constructions discussed above therefore fall into three categories. The first (the Bohr
analogue) is the definitional anchor. The second and third (the UPL applied to Earth, and the
kinetic-energy proximity to ) are epoch-independent relations that follow from the Moon's
mass. The fourth (the kinetic-energy form) is an epoch-dependent empirical fit. The convergence
of all four on a value near one second at the present epoch is a consequence of the framework's
eigenvalue and the specific historical position of the Moon. It is not evidence that the second is a

8. Tests and Falsifiability
8.1 The problem of testability
The filter hypothesis is a claim about the population of planetary systems. To test it, one needs a
sample of habitable-zone planets with measured satellite masses and a measure of habitability.
Neither is currently available. The hypothesis is therefore not testable with present data.
This does not make it unscientific. It makes it premature. The hypothesis makes specific
predictions about what future data should show, and the predictions are falsifiable in principle.
The purpose of this section is to state them clearly so that they can be tested when the data arrive.
8.2 Test 1: exomoon statistics
If the filter hypothesis is correct, habitable-zone terrestrial planets with large moons should be
overrepresented among planets with biosignatures, relative to the general population.
This requires a sample of exomoons, which does not yet exist. The detection of even a handful of
exomoons around habitable-zone planets would begin to constrain the hypothesis. The relevant
instruments are JWST (transit timing variations), PLATO (photometric precision), and the next
generation of space telescopes (direct imaging, high-contrast spectroscopy).
The prediction is specific: among habitable-zone planets with measured atmospheres, the
fraction with biosignatures should be higher for systems with a satellite-to-planet mass ratio
above than for systems below it.
8.3 Test 2: obliquity stability as a proxy
For exoplanets without detectable moons, obliquity stability can in principle be inferred from
photometric variability and from the planet's orbital architecture. A planet with a stable obliquity
will show a periodic photometric signature (from the obliquity-driven seasonal cycle); a planet
with a chaotic obliquity will show irregular variability.
If the filter hypothesis is correct, planets with stable obliquities should be more likely to show
biosignatures than planets with unstable ones, independently of whether a moon is detected.
This test does not require exomoon detection, and it is within reach of current instruments. The
challenge is distinguishing obliquity-driven variability from other sources of photometric
variation (stellar activity, weather, clouds). The test would require a sample of planets with well-
characterised photometric variability and measured atmospheric properties.
